newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Holiday mood hits index options.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Holiday mood hits index options.

text.p: A full trading session remains before Monday's Memorial Day holiday in the United States, but traders said major U.S. index options activity Thursday reminded them of pre-holiday trading.

"It's a deadly quiet day," said Jay Shartsis, head of options trading at R.F. Lafferty & Co in New York. "I guess it's the holiday manifesting itself. It feels like what I thought tomorrow would be like."
U.S. financial markets will be closed Monday.

One index options trader in Chicago said investors were happy to move to the sidelines after the week's excitement, which included Tuesday's Federal Reserve policy meeting where rates were left unchanged and a rally in technology stocks.
The fire in tech stocks was lit by Dell Computer Corp, which late Tuesday reported stronger than expected quarterly earnings and announced a two-for-one stock split.
"The Fed's done, so all the anticipation and speculation is gone," a trader of S&P 500 index .SPX futures-options said.
"It's a yawner to say the least," he said.
Shartsis said the euphoria over the Dell news, combined with some fairly robust index call buying recently, could indicate the market has formed a near-term top.
"I would think the hysteria associated with Dell probably put the market into a short-term topping position," he said.
"The market could come down," he added. "There's been quite a bit of call buying over the last few days and this morning there's still a fair amount of call buying."
He said the market, down moderately around midday Thursday, could remain weak through early Friday.
At about 1130 CDT/1630 GMT, the Dow industrial average was down 27 at 7,263. The SPX was off 2.24 at 837.11 and the S&P 100 index .OEX was down 3.25 at 822.93.
Short-term top or not, the market is seen as having a good chance of rising next week, based on historical patterns.
According to data from the Hirsch Organization, the market as measured by the Dow has been up the week after the Memorial Day holiday in 11 of the last 12 years.
The exception was 1996 when the blue chip barometer fell 2.1 percent in the four trading days after the holiday, Hirsch said.

According to Hirsch's Stock Traders Almanac, the Memorial Day rally last year failed to materialize because of the threat of higher interest rates and the market's high on May 22. For this year, it advised caution.

"It's always dangerous to publicize a favorable seasonal pattern," the Almanac said. "A pattern that has been in effect for a long time is bound to attract a multitude of traders, who will obviously want to take advantage of this bullish phenomenon."
